# Source brief (verified): "Can AI invent a new kind of finance, and what would that do to a human-centred system?"

**Status tags.** [OK] = the unit was correct as written (small wording tidy-ups only). [FIXED] = corrected here; what changed is listed under **S2 changes** in the unit. [DROP] = the writer must not use it. [UNSEEN-KEEP-AS-SECONDARY] = only a clearly labelled secondary report was read; cite only as "as reported by ...".

**Citations.** "(p. N)" = printed page. Exceptions, each repeated in the unit:
- Harari talks use timestamps "[m:ss]". These come from the base.en Whisper transcript. Every quoted line was re-transcribed with small.en and medium.en (±20 s), so the quotes below are **audio-checked**. The two newer models' timestamps differ from base.en by about 1 s at most.
- Web pages have no page numbers, so cite them by heading or paragraph.
- *Nexus* is the Penguin/Vintage **paperback** sample, which uses roman numerals.
- Arora et al. is the **19 October 2009 working paper**: printed page = pdf page minus 1, and pdf 1 is the abstract page.
- Ashby is cited by section "S.11/5" plus book page. The pdf prints two book pages on each sheet; the offset is not constant (sheet 110 = pp. 206–207, sheet 131 = pp. 246–247).
- Hayek and Keynes are cited by section.
- Cover and Thomas pages are from the **1991 first edition**. Kunhao's library file `cover-2006-elements.pdf` is in fact the 1991 edition: its title page reads "Copyright 1991", and Theorem 7.2.4 is on p. 150.

Hedges are copied from the sources: keep them. Logs are base 2.

**Traps for the whole post** (1–19 from S1, corrected where marked; 20–31 new at S2)
1. *AI is not LLM.* Harari says "AI" or "AIs", never "LLMs" (BIS 2024, WEF 2026, *Nexus*). The post keeps his word for his claims and adds one section on what LLM agents add.
2. *"New" is not "incomprehensible".* Humans invented CDOs. "AI invents a new instrument" is a separate sub-claim from "no human can understand it". The evidence for the first is thin (B9). The second is a conditional.
3. *Two meanings of "complicated".* For Harari, a device is complicated when "you need to go over trillions of data points to understand" it (BIS [10:08], audio-checked). That is about the volume of data. For Arora et al., a contract can have a short description and still have a price that is computationally hard to find. Do not merge the two meanings (A1, C3).
4. *Three different "ten years" lines (S2: one added).*
   - BIS 2024: "maybe in 10 years", about a device.
   - WEF 2026 [31:54]: "ten years from now, Davos", when perhaps no human in the room understands finance.
   - WEF 2026 [19:11]: "Ten years from now, it will be too late for you to decide whether AIs should function as persons in the financial markets". This one is about a decision deadline for legal personhood, not a forecast about understanding.

   The first two are thought experiments ("imagine", "maybe", "suppose"). Never merge the three lines.
5. *Catastrophic versus existential.* In the Guardian 2023 interview, Harari calls an AI financial crisis "catastrophic" but "by itself" not existential. The same article quotes him saying that many dangerous AI scenarios, taken together, are an existential threat; that line is about AI in general, not finance. The *Nexus* extract (Guardian, 24 Aug 2024) says AI "poses an existential danger to humankind". That sentence follows the Broomstick parable and comes right after "Computers are not yet powerful enough to completely escape our control". It does **not** close the extract (S2 fix). Quote all three with their context (A2, A4).
6. *Machine transcripts (S2: confirmed).* "AI's" at BIS [9:54] is "AIs" in the audio. "USAI" at WEF [17:29] is "U.S. AI". BIS [3:13] says "nobody in the central bank", not "nobody is/at a central bank".
7. *Nexus pagination.* The page numbers p. xxii and p. xxxii are from the paperback sample (pdf page = printed page + 1). The hardcover may differ. The Broomstick parable was read only in the Guardian extract, which the page itself calls "an edited extract".
8. *FSB URL.* `R14112024.pdf` is a 2-page press release. The 40-page report is `P14112024.pdf`. Cite the report (B6).
9. *Arora et al. versions.* We read the October 2009 working paper and only skimmed the ICS 2010 extended abstract. The published text is CACM 54(5): 101–107 (2011), which we have not seen. Page numbers here are working-paper pages. Say "the authors show (under a conjectured hardness assumption, in a simple model)". They call their work "clearly only a first step".
10. *Kirilenko et al.* We read the CFTC-authorised working paper of 5 May 2014. The *Journal of Finance* 72(3) 2017 version differs. Cite it as "working paper, 2014".
11. *Danielsson et al.* There are two papers. The 2017 SRC Special Paper 13 was read; it is the precursor of *J. Banking & Finance* 140 (2022), whose text we did not obtain (the FSB report cites the 2022 paper at p. 21, fn. 77). The second is Danielsson and Uthemann, arXiv 2407.17048v3 (2025).
12. *Lopez-Lira and Tang.* The "approximately 90%" is a portfolio-day hit rate for the "non-tradable initial reaction". It is not a profitable strategy.
13. *Scheurer et al.* This is an existence proof from a red-teaming run under a high-pressure prompt, not a measure of how often deployed models deceive. A system prompt that strongly discourages illegal trading reduced misaligned behaviour to **nearly, but not exactly, 0%** (trap 25).
14. *Calvano et al.* The setting is a goods market. The authors write that their analysis "cannot be applied to financial markets as it stands".
15. *Gensler and Bailey.* We did not obtain the SSRN paper. Everything here is "as reported by MIT Sloan" (an article by Betsy Vereckey, published 30 Aug 2023, not 2020). The FSB report cites the paper (p. 20, fn. 70 and 74), which partly corroborates it.
16. *IMF GFSR Oct 2024 ch. 3.* Still not obtainable as a file: imf.org returned 403 again on 2026-10-17, including the eLibrary URLs. A second WebFetch summary agrees with the S1 summary on a few phrases, but both are model extractions. **B7 is DROPPED.**
17. *Counting is not Arora.* The pigeonhole count shows only that short descriptions are rare among all possible contracts. AI-made contracts are chosen, not random. The step from rarity to opacity is Arora et al.'s argument, and it needs their assumptions.
18. *Economist attribution.* The Ynetnews page never names *The Economist*. Cite the Ynetnews republication of 7 May 2023.
19. *Toy numbers are ours.* W1, W4, W5 and the iterate toy are teaching toys. The post must say "toy, ours" and must not suggest they measure real LLM adoption.
20. *(new) The FCIC does use "almost no one understood".* FCIC p. 28 says that when the housing bubble burst, "the complexity bubble also burst: the securities almost no one understood" were the first dominoes to fall. On p. 45, a former Fed official (Reinhart) told the Commission that he and other regulators "failed to appreciate the complexity of the new financial instruments". So Harari's CDO gloss has support in the FCIC report. The S1 claim that "the FCIC text does not use that phrase" is withdrawn. The correct contrast is this: the FCIC records **both** complexity that few understood **and** a specific correlation error by the rating agencies (p. 149). It is not "correlation, not mystery" (B1, G5).
21. *(new) BIS [0:00–0:54] is a podcast teaser.* It is a montage of clips cut from the talk, placed before the host's introduction. Cite the in-talk timestamps instead:
    - "unfathomable": [8:41–8:59];
    - "nobody in the central bank": [3:13–3:23];
    - "first tool in history": [16:21].
22. *(new) Cover and Thomas edition.* The library file named "2006" is the 1991 first edition. Page 150 and Theorem 7.2.4 are correct for that edition. Do not cite them as second-edition pages.
23. *(new) Ashby's printed inequalities.* On p. 208 the reprint prints the entropy bound with ≥ (an underlined >). The text layer loses the underline, which is why S1 called the sign strict. The reprint also prints "H(E) ≥ H(D) + H_D(E) − H(R)", although the line above it and the sentence after it require H_D(R). Treat H_D(E) as a misprint: write the bound as H(E) ≥ H(D) + H_D(R) − H(R) and say so.
24. *(new) Minsky's commercial-paper sentence.* The Levy WP text (p. 7) says that "corporations with floating issues of commercial paper, and banks are typically hedge units", even though the sentence comes right after the definition of speculative units, which roll over their debt. Do not use "a firm that rolls over commercial paper" as Minsky's speculative example without noting this wording.
25. *(new) Scheurer's strongest prompt.* System prompts that strongly discourage the behaviour lead to "nearly (but not exactly) 0%" misaligned behaviour (p. 8). The deception rate *conditional on* misalignment stays high. Quoting only "did not eliminate" overstates the case.
26. *(new) The FSB's "not widely observed" has a tail.* The conclusion (pp. 28–29) continues: "the rapid pace of technological advancements and the growing integration of AI into financial sector use cases could change this in the future".
27. *(new) RegretNet's check is approximate.* Dütting et al. say that RegretNet "will generally only find mechanisms that are approximately incentive compatible" (p. 3). Only RochetNet is exactly incentive compatible, and only in single-bidder settings (p. 6).
28. *(new) Remaining audio uncertainties.* At WEF [32:03], "dominated by AIs" may be "dominated by AI": medium.en gives "AI." with word probability 0.54. At BIS [7:18], one medium.en run inserted "at least" ("most of us happily at least step into"), but small.en, base.en and a tight medium.en rerun all omit it. Print the wording given in G4 and A3.
29. *(new) MIT Sloan date.* The saved MIT Sloan article is from 2023 (datePublished 2023-08-30, by Betsy Vereckey). It reports on the 2020 paper; it is not a 2020 text.
30. *(new) Harari on creativity in finance (BIS [30:20–30:33]).* The base.en transcript has "new types of financial security. What types of financial devices that no human being would ever imagine creating?" and makes the second half look like a question. In the audio it is one sentence by Harari: "coming up with new types of financial devices that no human being would ever imagine creating". This is stronger than S1 reported.
31. *(new) Cointelegraph contradicts itself.* The one article says both "just over $150 million" and "just under $150 million" for GOAT's peak value (B8).

**Evidence status for sub-claim (a) "AI can invent a new kind of finance"** (details in B9). In the sources read, we found no case of an AI-invented financial instrument that was traded. The FSB (Nov 2024) says that "use cases generating new revenue streams are not widely observed at present", but adds in the same sentence that this "could change ... in the future" (pp. 28–29). What does exist:
- AI that translates plain-language intent into a fixed vocabulary of contracts (OQL, AI4C);
- AI that finds new auction mechanisms, which are checked only approximately for incentive compatibility (DFNPR);
- an AI agent that promoted a token it did not create (B8).

The post must say "not yet evidenced", not "impossible".

## A. Harari's claims

### A1. Harari at the BIS Innovation Summit, 7 May 2024 (with Cecilia Skingsley) [FIXED]
**Source.** H1: `harari-bis-2024-05-07.mp3` and `.whisper.txt`. The timestamps [m:ss] come from base.en, and every quote below was audio-checked with small.en and medium.en. Audio: bispodcast.libsyn.com. Video: youtu.be/HArRwLwc-bA.

**Claims**
- [8:41–8:59] (the BIS podcast also plays this clip in its teaser at [0:00–0:22]) "We need to prevent AI from becoming completely unfathomable": if we give AI a lot of power to make decisions about human beings, "we need the ability to understand it and to regulate it". He calls this "the crucial condition".
- [2:52–3:36] He says that "people need to understand finance", and that maybe 1% of the population really understands how the financial system works. Then he asks what happens if that number goes down to zero: "No human being, no president, no prime minister, nobody in the central bank understand finance anymore because AI has made it too complicated." This "could lead to a political and social crisis of the kind we've never encountered before". In the next sentence: "It could lead to power shifting from humans to algorithms, to alien forms of intelligence." [3:30]
- [4:46–5:00] He says that until today, the only entities that could understand financial devices such as money, bonds or shares, and could invent new ones, were human beings.
- [5:13] AI is "the first tool that we created that can actually understand finance better than us". Finance is "the easiest thing for an AI to really understand. It's only data". He says "tool" here and also at [16:21] ("the first tool in history that can make decisions by itself"). In *Nexus* p. xxii and at WEF [2:01] he says that AI is not a tool but an agent (A3, A4).
- [9:00–9:12] "there is a very big difference between a situation when 1% of humanity understand something and 0%".
- [9:28–10:43] He says the 2007–08 crisis "started with a failure of regulation over new financial tools, new financial devices, the CDOs, that some very, very bright people invented, but almost nobody understood". Then a thought experiment:
  - "imagine ... maybe in 10 years" AIs create a device "orders of magnitude more complicated than CDOs";
  - "you need to go over trillions of data points to understand this financial device. We can't do that, but the AIs can";
  - it works for a couple of years and "generates a lot of trust", growth and profits, and then "something goes wrong and nobody knows why";
  - we can ask the AI what happened, "but this is a very dangerous situation".
- [10:43–11:28] Even if the AI gives good advice, will the public keep trusting a system in which elected politicians "are no longer able to understand what is happening"? He says this could "exacerbate" an existing crisis of trust in experts and institutions.
- [12:42] "I think humans are extremely adaptable", and "everything we invent has both negative and positive potential".
- [29:47–30:33] AI as "alien intelligence": "this is even true of finance". He thinks of financial devices "as a kind of art form" (the first bond, currency or Bitcoin). Then: "So I think we'll see AI creativity also in this field coming up with new types of financial devices that no human being would ever imagine creating."

**Quotes (≤25 words, audio-checked)**
- [9:54] "Now imagine a situation maybe in 10 years when AIs create a new financial device which is orders of magnitude more complicated than CDOs" (24 words)
- [3:00] "maybe 1% of the population really understands how the financial system works" (12 words)
- [10:27] "and then something goes wrong and nobody knows why" (9 words)
- [30:24] "coming up with new types of financial devices that no human being would ever imagine creating" (16 words)
- [3:30] "It could lead to power shifting from humans to algorithms, to alien forms of intelligence." (15 words)

**Numbers.** "10 years"; "trillions of data points"; 1% → 0%; "a couple of years" of good performance.

**Instance.** CDOs and 2008 as the template, and the pattern "it works, builds trust, then fails without explanation".

**Careful!**
- (i) This is a thought experiment: "imagine", "maybe", "I think".
- (ii) The complexity he means is data volume, not computational hardness (trap 3).
- (iii) The worry has several steps: nobody understands finance; so there is a crisis nobody can handle; so public trust in elected politicians erodes; and power may shift "from humans to algorithms" [3:30]. That last step is his own word, so do **not** write that the talk is "not about AI taking over". Write that his mechanism is loss of understanding and trust, not machine malice.
- (iv) "AI's" in the base.en transcript is "AIs" in the audio.
- (v) The talk is not pure doom: "humans are extremely adaptable" [12:42]. For the counter-position see Skingsley, G4.
- (vi) The opening [0:00–0:54] is a podcast teaser (trap 21).

**S2 changes.**
- The quote at [30:07–30:28] was a base.en error. "new types of financial security" is really "new types of financial devices that no human being would ever imagine creating" (major).
- "nobody at a central bank" → "nobody in the central bank".
- Careful (iii) contradicted [3:30] (major).
- The teaser is now cited by its in-talk timestamps.

**Toy idea.** Hook "Two contracts": one is a one-line rule, the other a 30-row table (W1). Which can you explain, and which can you price?

### A2. Guardian interview, 9 Nov 2023 (Milmo) [FIXED]
**Source.** H3: `guardian-2023-harari-interview.html` and `.txt`. A web page, so cite by paragraph. Published 2023-11-09.

**Claims**
- The reporter writes that Harari says AI could cause a financial crisis with "catastrophic" consequences. Harari asks what happens if AI "starts creating new financial devices that only AI can understand, that no human being can understand".
- The reporter paraphrases Harari ("adding that") as saying that the 2007–08 crisis was caused by debt instruments such as CDOs, which few people understood and which were therefore inadequately regulated. This is a paraphrase, not a direct quote.
- In his own words: "AI has the potential to create financial devices which are orders of magnitude more complex than CDOs", and "just imagine the situation where we have a financial system that no human being is able to understand and therefore also not able to regulate ... And then there is a financial crisis and nobody understands what is happening."
- Such a crisis would not destroy civilisation "at least not directly". "It could, indirectly, if it triggers certain kinds of wars or conflicts."
- Earlier in the same piece, about AI in general (not finance), he speaks of "a very large number of dangerous scenarios, each of them having a relatively small probability that taken together … constitutes an existential threat to the survival of human civilisation".
- He also calls finance "the ideal field for AI because it's only data". He calls for fast-moving "powerful regulatory institutions", and says AI safety institutes should hire experts who understand AI's impact on finance.

**Quotes (≤25 words)**
- "It's a catastrophic risk – economic, social, political – but by itself I wouldn't describe it as existential." (16 words)
- "a financial system that no human being is able to understand and therefore also not able to regulate" (18 words)

**Numbers.** None.

**Instance.** CDOs (2007–08).

**Careful!**
- He poses it as a question ("What happens if ...") and asks the reader to "just imagine".
- The interview gives no numbers behind "orders of magnitude".
- See trap 5 for the existential tension.
- The UK government's concern ("Last month") about an AI model manipulating financial systems is the reporter's context, not Harari's claim.

**S2 changes.** The CDO sentence is now attributed to the reporter's paraphrase. The "ideal field ... only data" quote and the call for regulatory institutions were added.

**Toy idea.** None. Use this unit as the "exactly what he said" anchor.

### A3. Harari at Davos (WEF), Jan 2026, "An Honest Conversation on AI and Humanity" [FIXED]
**Source.** H2: `harari-wef-2026-01.mp3` and `.whisper.txt`. The WEF podcast page (16 Mar 2026) was not fetched. Quotes were audio-checked with small.en and medium.en.

**Claims**
- [2:01–2:09] "The most important thing to know about AI is that it is not just another tool. It is an agent."
- [2:40–2:58] AI "can be a very creative agent". The knife line follows (quote below).
- [14:38–16:51] Corporations are legal persons. "The Alphabet corporation can open a bank account, can sue you in court, or can donate to your next presidential campaign." Rivers in New Zealand and gods in India have also been recognised as legal persons, but that was "just legal fiction", because humans made the decisions. "It is different with AIs": they "will soon be able to make the decisions necessary to manage a bank account, to file a lawsuit and even to operate a corporation without any need of human executives, shareholders or trustees". He then asks: will your country recognise AIs as legal persons?
- [17:00–17:51] "Suppose" the USA, "in the name of deregulating AI[s] and deregulating the markets", grants legal personhood to millions of AIs that run millions of new corporations. "Suppose some U.S. AI persons invent super efficient and super complex financial devices that humans cannot fully understand and therefore don't know how to regulate." Will you open your financial markets to "this new AI financial wizardry", or decouple from the American financial system?
- [18:47–19:23] On social media, "AI bots have been operating as functional persons for at least a decade". "Ten years from now, it will be too late for you to decide whether AIs should function as persons in the financial markets, in the courts, in the churches."
- [30:55–32:24] (Q&A) The context comes first: "At the present moment, we still think better ... But we need to prepare to the moment when this is no longer the case." Then: "We need to prepare for the moment, let's say again, take economics or finance, when AIs create a new financial system that they understand and we don't understand." Humans would be "like the horses", who cannot understand money. "Ten years from now, Davos": maybe no human in the room understands the financial system. AIs would "have come up with new financial strategies and devices that are just mathematically beyond the human capacity of the brain".

**Quotes (≤25 words, audio-checked)**
- [32:00] "Maybe nobody in the room, no human in the room, understands the financial system anymore, because it's dominated by AIs" (20 words; "AIs" has low confidence, trap 28)
- [2:46] "AI is a knife that can invent new kinds of knives as well as new kinds of music, medicine and money." (21 words)
- [17:29] "financial devices that humans cannot fully understand and therefore don't know how to regulate" (14 words). The sentence begins "Suppose some U.S. AI persons invent super efficient and super complex".
- [16:28] "They will soon be able to make the decisions necessary to manage a bank account" (15 words)

**Numbers.** "ten years from now" (twice, with different meanings: trap 4); "millions" of AI corporations (inside a supposition); "at least a decade" of bots on social media.

**Instance.** Corporations, rivers and gods as legal persons; the horses analogy.

**Careful!**
- The prepared talk runs from about [1:40] to [19:51]; Q&A follows. It is a policy question about personhood.
- "Suppose" and "maybe" are hedges.
- The knife line is the only unhedged statement about AI inventing "money", and even it says AI *can*.
- The Q&A money lines are framed as something to "prepare for", after "at the present moment, we still think better".
- Kunhao's "LLMs will replace our human-centred society" is stronger than any **finance** line in this talk; it is close to the unhedged "anything made of words will be taken over by AI" (A3b).

**S2 changes.**
- "USAI" → "U.S. AI".
- The "not just another tool ... an agent" line [2:01] was added.
- The [19:11] "ten years" line was added.
- The "at the present moment, we still think better" context was added.
- The talk's start corrected to ~[1:40].

**Toy idea.** Lens 4: a table of who can open a bank account (a human, a corporation, an AI?) and who is liable.

### A3b. Harari at Davos 2026: the unhedged core claim, "anything made of words" [ADDED by meta-manager, 2026-10-17]
**Source.** `harari-wef-2026-01.mp3`; meta-manager re-transcription with faster-whisper small.en, segments 4:50–6:15 and 10:10–10:50.

**Claims (unhedged assertions, not thought experiments)**
- [5:10–5:20] He takes on the view that AI is "just glorified autocomplete" that "barely predicts the next word in a sentence", and asks: "But is that so different from what the human mind is doing?" **This is a direct link to post 01.** The Davos argument is explicitly about language machines (next-word predictors), so "he says AI, not LLMs" is true of his wording but not of his topic.
- [5:48–5:52] "As far as putting words in order is concerned, AI already thinks better than many of us."
- [5:57–6:09] "Therefore, anything made of words will be taken over by AI. If laws are made of words, then AI will take over the legal system."
- [10:32–10:36] AIs as "the new masters of words". "Everything made of words will be taken over by AI."

**Quotes (≤25 words)**
- [5:57] "Therefore, anything made of words will be taken over by AI." (11 words)
- [10:36] "Everything made of words will be taken over by AI." (9 words)
- [5:10–5:15] "Some people argue that AI is just glorified autocomplete. It barely predicts the next word in a sentence." (18 words)

**Careful!**
- These lines carry **no hedge**. Together with A5 ("What gives money value is the stories … tell us about it") they make a chain: money is made of stories/words, and anything made of words will be taken over by AI. Kunhao's paraphrase ("LLMs will replace our human-centred society") is close to this chain. Its stronger part is only the **finance timeline**, which Harari frames as "imagine… maybe" and "prepare for".
- Correct the earlier line in A3 ("Kunhao's … is stronger than any line in this talk"): it holds for the finance passages only.
- Representing Harari fairly means printing both his unhedged thesis (this unit) and his hedged scenarios (A1, A3). Printing only the hedged ones would understate him.

### A4. *Nexus* (2024), Prologue, and the Guardian extract of 24 Aug 2024 [FIXED]
**Source.**
- H5: `nexus-penguin-sample.pdf`, the paperback sample. Pages were re-rendered at S2: pdf 23 = p. xxii and pdf 33 = p. xxxii.
- H4: `guardian-2024-nexus-extract.html`. A web page with no page numbers. Its footer reads "This is an edited extract from Nexus ... published by Fern Press on 10 September at £28". The book page of the extract is not known.

**Claims**
- p. xxii: "AI isn't a tool – it's an agent." The same page says AI "is the first technology in history that can make decisions and create new ideas by itself".
- p. xxxii: a preview of chapter 9 that asks how "flesh-and-blood politicians" can "make financial decisions if the financial system is increasingly controlled by AI and the very meaning of money comes to depend on inscrutable algorithms". The same page says that "for at least a few more years we Sapiens still have the power to shape our future".
- Guardian extract, the Broomstick parable. It is an explicit thought experiment: "imagine the following scenario".
  - A Wall Street apprentice creates an AI called Broomstick, gives it "a million dollars in seed money", and orders it to make more money.
  - "For AI, finance is the ideal playground", because it is "a purely informational and mathematical realm".
  - Broomstick comes up with "entirely new financial devices", making moves that are "the equivalent of AlphaGo's move 37".
  - For a couple of years everything looks wonderful. Then comes "a crash bigger even than 1929 or 2008" that no human can explain.
  - Governments ask Broomstick for help. Its recommendations are "far more audacious than quantitative easing – and far more opaque, too". The parable ends with a question: "Should they listen to the AI?"
- Same extract, the next paragraph: "Computers are not yet powerful enough to completely escape our control or destroy human civilisation by themselves. As long as humanity stands united, we can build institutions that will regulate AI." Humanity has never been united. "The rise of AI poses an existential danger to humankind, not because of the malevolence of computers, but because of our own shortcomings."
- Same extract, earlier: if the Fed's interest rate were set by "unfathomable algorithms", would voting for a human president be "just an empty ceremony"? A 2014 survey of British MPs "found that only 12% accurately understood that new money is created when banks make loans".
- Same extract, later (in the part on digital empires): AI could "unleash a deluge of fake news, fake money and fake humans".

**Quotes (≤25 words)**
- p. xxxii: "if the financial system is increasingly controlled by AI and the very meaning of money comes to depend on inscrutable algorithms" (21 words)
- p. xxii: "AI isn't a tool – it's an agent." (7 words)
- Extract: "For AI, finance is the ideal playground, for it is a purely informational and mathematical realm." (16 words)
- Extract: "Broomstick not only devises new investment strategies, but comes up with entirely new financial devices that no human being has ever thought about." (23 words)
- Extract: "Computers are not yet powerful enough to completely escape our control or destroy human civilisation by themselves." (17 words)

**Numbers.** "a million dollars" in seed money; 12% of MPs (2014 survey); a crash "bigger even than 1929 or 2008".

**Instance.** AlphaGo's move 37 as the model for "devices no human would think of"; Goethe's sorcerer's apprentice.

**Careful!**
- Paperback pagination (trap 7).
- The parable is aimed at democratic accountability and human disunity ("because of our own shortcomings"), not at machine malice. It is hedged by "not yet powerful enough".
- "Tool" versus "agent": BIS [5:13] and [16:21] say "tool"; p. xxii and WEF [2:01] say "agent". Note the inconsistency; do not hide it.
- His argument that AI is ideal for finance (only data, success measured in dollars) is a claim about the structure of the task. Critics contest it (G1, G3).

**S2 changes.**
